chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
title: A real school of jazz: faculty, students and Paul Jeffries
summary: Mingus says the music is taught mainly to white players, names ideal teachers, and says composition cannot be taught.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah. You mentioned before -- Ornette reminded me, that school of jazz they had was Lennox Inn, in the Berkshires, where -- John Lewis was teaching there and Gunther (Schweller) and all that. And it seemed to generate some excitment and then disappeared. Do you think that's feasible, someday having -- like, they have the Manhatten School of Music, the Juilliard or Rochester, having a really first class school of jazz? Can it be -- it's the old cliche question, can it be taught?
Well, it's being taught to the white guys.
Yeah.
They get jobs in (unintelligible) all-white bands.
Yeah.
Al Ferguson (unintelligible) young guys.
Would he? There again, it's a suppo-
sition thing. Suppose you were running such a place, or advising somebody who's running it, what would the faculty be? What would their responsibilities be?
I would have Sonny Rollins, Buddy Colette, somebody who could teach classical fundamentals, as well as jazz improvisation.
Yeah.
And jazz composition.
And how would you decide on how to select students? What would they have to show, and how could you measure their potential? Suppose they didn't have any background?

Well, I'll give you an idea. There's a guy came to the club, wanted to see my man on tenor saxophone. Man, he couldn't play nothing, didn't know no tunes or nothing. So I said, can you play by yourself? And we left the man standing, he played by hisself. And he composed. He cut George Adams, just making up things by hisself.
Yeah.
He came by about a week ago. I told him to go home and study, what to study. He's got to learn how to read, he's got to learn (inaudible) composition.
Yeah.
And what you're doing on your own, keep doing on your own. So he came over here to play some of his
compositions. The main thing is when you find a student that's got a compositional ear, compositional soul, (inaudible), teach him all the techniques you can. Composition is not taught, really.
Yeah.
(Unintelligible) composition. If a guy has got it, he's got it.

Would you like to see that, though, the kind of school that I mentioned, a really good school with the kind of faculty you're talking about? Because we've never had it, except for that brief couple of summers at Lennox.
I think Paul Jeffries has got one.
Oh, yeah?
You know Paul Jeffries?
Yeah, I know who he is, of course.
He has a school on -- Sue?
Yeah.
Where's Paul's school? You want some wine, man?
Yeah.
(Inaudible.)
You want some wine?
Yeah, sure.
Hey, Sue.
Yeah.
Me and Nat want some wine.
Oh, that's --
How about some cheese? (Inaudible.)
I can talk better on wine.
